In 2007, 2013 and 2020, the EU Labour Force Survey asked workers in every European country
whether they had an accident at work in the past year, whether work had caused or worsened a
health problem, and what risk factors they were exposed to at work. This notebook uses Eurostat's
40 tables from those surveys. Read the module [README](../README.md) and
[data dictionary](../data_dictionary.md) first.

**How to use this notebook**

- Run each code chunk in order (the green arrow in RStudio, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter).
- Answer the questions under each **Your answer** heading.
- When you are done, click **Knit** to produce an HTML report to submit.

# Part 0. Load the data

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(forcats)

base <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eddiekasner/occupational-safety-health-datasets/main/modules/intl-eurostat-lfs-health/data"
read_module <- function(folder, name, ...) {
  local <- file.path("..", "data", folder, name)
  read_csv(if (file.exists(local)) local else file.path(base, folder, name), show_col_types = FALSE,
           ...)
}

# The 40 Eurostat tables, and the values from each
tables <- read_module("tidy", "tables.csv")
accidents <- read_module("tidy", "accidents.csv.gz")
health <- read_module("tidy", "health_problems.csv.gz")
exposures <- read_module("tidy", "exposures.csv.gz")

# Countries only (no EU or euro area aggregates)
aggregates <- c("EU27_2020", "EU28", "EA19")
```

Every value is a **percentage**. Each table repeats the headline figures, so always pick one
`table` at a time, and use the age group `15-64`, which every table has. The `flag` column marks
values with low reliability (`u`) or breaks in series (`b`).

# Part 1. How common are accidents and health problems?

```{r headline}
bind_rows(accidents |> filter(table == "hsw_ac1"), health |> filter(table == "hsw_pb1")) |>
  filter(geo == "EU27_2020", age == "15-64", category_code == "TOTAL") |>
  select(measure, year, sex, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = value)
```

**Questions**

1. About what percentage of EU workers report an accident at work in a year, and a work-related
   health problem? Which is more common?
2. Men report more accidents and women more health problems. Suggest reasons, thinking about the
   jobs men and women do.
3. Administrative statistics count only accidents that lead to more than three days off work (see
   the ESAW module). Why would a survey find more accidents than an employer reporting system?

**Your answer:**



# Part 2. Comparing countries

```{r countries}
accidents |>
  filter(table == "hsw_ac1", year == 2020, sex == "Total", age == "15-64",
         category_code == "TOTAL", !geo %in% aggregates) |>
  ggplot(aes(value, fct_reorder(country, value), fill = flag == "u")) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey40", `TRUE` = "orange"),
                    labels = c("Reliable", "Low reliability"), na.translate = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "People reporting an accident at work in the past 12 months, 2020",
       x = "Percentage of people working in the past 12 months", y = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

**Questions**

1. Which countries report the most and the fewest accidents at work? How many times higher is the
   highest than the lowest?
2. Is it plausible that work in Finland is many times more dangerous than in Lithuania? List
   reasons why people in some countries might be more likely to report an accident in a survey.
3. What would you need to know before using these figures to rank countries by safety?

**Your answer:**

```{r activities}
health |>
```

# Part 4. Types of health problem

```{r health-types}
health |>
  filter(table == "hsw_pb5", geo == "EU27_2020", sex != "Total", age == "15-64",
         year == 2020, unit == "PC_PER_HPB") |>
  ggplot(aes(value, fct_reorder(category, value), fill = sex)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Most serious work-related health problem, EU, 2020",
       x = "Percentage of people with a work-related health problem", y = NULL, fill = NULL)

health |>
  filter(table == "hsw_pb3", geo == "EU27_2020", age == "15-64", unit == "PC_PER_HPB") |>
  select(category, year, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = value)
```

**Questions**

1. What are the two most common types of work-related health problem? Do men and women differ?
2. About what share of people with a work-related health problem were off work for a month or
   more? What does that suggest about the cost of these problems?
3. Most of these health problems are not recognised occupational diseases. Why might a
   musculoskeletal disorder that a worker attributes to work never be compensated?

**Your answer:**



# Part 5. Exposure to risk factors

```{r exposures}
exposures |>
  filter(table %in% c("hsw_exp3", "hsw_exp4"), geo == "EU27_2020", sex != "Total",
         age == "15-64", year == 2020) |>
  ggplot(aes(value, fct_reorder(category, value), fill = sex)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  facet_wrap(~ measure, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Main risk factor at work, EU, 2020", x = "Percentage of people working",
       y = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

**Questions**

1. What is the most common main risk factor for physical health, and for mental well-being? Where
   do men and women differ most?
2. Time pressure or overload of work is the most common main risk factor for mental well-being.
   Which jobs would you expect to have the most, and what organisational changes could reduce it?

**Your answer:**



# Part 6. When the question changes (ENVH 460/560)

```{r question-change}
exposures |>
  filter(table %in% c("hsw_exp1", "hsw_exp2"), geo == "EU27_2020", sex == "Total",

exposures |>
  filter(table == "hsw_exp3", geo == "EU27_2020", sex == "Total", age == "15-64") |>
  select(category, year, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = value)
```

# Part 7. Who is at risk (ENVH 460/560)

```{r inequalities}
accidents |>
  filter(table %in% c("hsw_ac1", "hsw_ac8", "hsw_ac12"), geo == "EU27_2020", sex == "Total",
         age == "15-64", year == 2020) |>
  select(breakdown, category, value, flag)

health |>
  filter(table == "hsw_pb1", geo == "EU27_2020", sex == "Total", age == "15-64") |>
  select(category, year, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = value)
```

**Questions**

1. How do accident rates differ by education level, professional status and country of birth?
   Which differences would you expect, and which surprise you?
2. Self-employed people report fewer accidents than employees. Give one explanation about risk and

# Part 8. How reliable are small numbers? (ENVH 460/560)

```{r reliability}
bind_rows(accidents, health, exposures) |>
  filter(year == 2020, !geo %in% aggregates) |>
  group_by(country) |>
  summarise(values = n(), low_reliability = mean(grepl("u", flag))) |>
  arrange(desc(low_reliability)) |>
  head(10)
```

**Questions**

1. Which countries have the highest share of low-reliability values? Why?
2. If you wanted to compare accident rates between construction workers in two small countries,
   what would you do about reliability?
3. Write a short paragraph for a policy maker on what self-reported surveys can tell them that
   administrative accident statistics cannot, and the reverse.
